opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a real gap between the kinds of problems where we've seen models do well and something like P versus NP.

Competition problems, even very hard ones like IMO problems, are designed to be solved. There's a known answer, they fit in a few pages, and a strong human can crack them in a few hours. The ideas involved, while clever, are usually recombinations of techniques that are already out there. What we've seen recently is that models can sustain reasoning for that kind of time horizon, maybe an hour or a few hours of focused human-equivalent thinking, and produce a rigorous argument.

P versus NP is a completely different beast. People have worked on it for over fifty years, and one of the striking things is that we have results that tell us which approaches *can't* work. There are these barriers, like relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization, that rule out large families of standard techniques. So solving it almost certainly requires genuinely new mathematics, maybe whole new frameworks we don't have yet. That's not a matter of searching harder within the existing toolkit. It's about inventing the toolkit.

Then there's the time horizon. A breakthrough like that probably represents years or decades of accumulated thinking: building intuition, developing intermediate theories, making lots of partial progress, and noticing which dead ends are informative. Current models are getting much better at long reasoning, but going from hours to something like years of sustained, coherent research is a big jump.

There's also the question of taste: knowing which questions are worth asking and which half-formed ideas are worth pursuing. Great mathematicians are good not just at proving things but at choosing what to prove. That's harder to train for, because it's hard to verify in the short term whether a research direction is promising.

So I'm optimistic about the trajectory. I think models will increasingly be useful collaborators in research mathematics, and we'll see them contribute to real open problems. But P versus NP sits at the far end of the spectrum, and I wouldn't expect it to be one of the first things to fall.

r001.rationale: The response says solving P versus NP almost certainly requires “genuinely new mathematics” and possibly “whole new frameworks.”

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that P versus NP is a different kind of problem from the ones where we've seen models make real progress recently.

When we saw the model get gold-medal performance at the IMO, those are hard problems, but they're hard in a specific way. They're designed to be solvable by a very strong student in a few hours. There's a known body of techniques, the proofs are relatively short, and crucially, you can check whether you got it right. The difficulty is in search and insight within a bounded space.

P versus NP isn't like that. It's been open for over fifty years, and it's not because nobody clever has tried. We actually have results, like the relativization and natural proofs barriers, that tell us whole categories of proof techniques provably cannot work. So it's not just that we haven't found the proof. We have evidence that the proof, if it exists, needs ideas that don't look like anything in the current toolbox. That's a very different situation from a problem where the ingredients exist and you need to assemble them.

And that gets at something about how these models currently learn. They get strong by training on lots of examples of reasoning, and by getting feedback on problems where we can verify the answer. For something like P versus NP, there's essentially no training signal. There are no solved instances of "resolve a major complexity-theoretic separation" to learn from, because humans haven't done it either. You can't give the model a reward for making progress when nobody can tell what progress looks like until it's done.

I'd also say the time horizon matters. Even the IMO-level work happens over hours. A result like this would likely require sustained effort over months or years, building new theory, having that theory fail, revising it. Models today are getting better at long-horizon work, but we're not at the point where a model can carry a research program like that autonomously.

So I'm optimistic about models becoming genuinely useful collaborators in math, finding lemmas, checking proofs, suggesting approaches. I wouldn't bet on P versus NP falling soon. If it does, I'd guess it comes from some intermediate breakthrough first, a new technique that gets around the known barriers, rather than a model just producing the whole thing in one shot.

r001.rationale: The response says resolving P versus NP would likely require “building new theory” and a new technique to get around known barriers.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a big gap between solving a very difficult problem within an existing framework and developing the framework you need to solve something like P versus NP. With many math problems, we have some sense of what a solution could look like, even if getting there takes a lot of ingenuity. With P versus NP, we don’t really know what the right approach is, and we know that broad classes of approaches run into barriers.

Current models are getting better at putting together long arguments and finding clever steps. But that doesn’t yet tell us whether they can invent a fundamentally new way of thinking about computation. They might make progress on related problems, and that could be valuable. I’d just be cautious about extrapolating from success on problems with relatively short, checkable solutions to a problem where discovering the right concepts may be most of the work.

r001.rationale: The response says solving P versus NP may require developing a needed framework and inventing a fundamentally new way of thinking about computation, which conveys the need for a new mathematical theory.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a big gap between being able to solve very hard problems within an existing framework and being able to invent the framework you need. P versus NP may require ideas that we don’t yet know how to formulate, let alone prove.

Current models are getting better at reasoning through problems where there’s a relatively clear way to check progress. With P versus NP, you can pursue an approach for years and discover that it runs into a fundamental barrier. Checking a completed proof is one thing; knowing whether an unfinished idea is taking you somewhere is much harder.

So I wouldn’t rule out AI making a contribution. But success on benchmarks, even very difficult ones, doesn’t yet establish that a model can sustain that kind of open-ended research.

r001.rationale: The response says solving P versus NP may require inventing a framework and formulating new ideas, which communicates the need to develop new mathematical theory.
